\section[ūndecim — vīgintī]{ūndecim, vīgintī — the source numbers, including a genuine oddity}

\label{lesson:LA-C16-undecim-viginti}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've seen Spanish's \emph{once} through \emph{quince} as fused, worn-down compounds. Here are the whole, un-fused Latin originals — plus a real quirk in Latin's own counting system that Spanish quietly dropped.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ūndecim–quīndecim — plain "X-ten" compounds}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{ūndecim} & \emph{ūnus} + \emph{decim}, "one-ten" \\
\textbf{duodecim} & \emph{duo} + \emph{decim}, "two-ten" \\
\textbf{tredecim} & \emph{trēs} + \emph{decim}, "three-ten" \\
\textbf{quattuordecim} & \emph{quattuor} + \emph{decim}, "four-ten" \\
\textbf{quīndecim} & \emph{quīnque} + \emph{decim}, "five-ten" \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Straightforward additive compounds — number, then \emph{decim} ("ten," from \textbf{decem}). These are the direct, whole ancestors of Spanish's \emph{once, doce, trece, catorce, quince} — fused down over the centuries into single words.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sēdecim, septendecim — still additive}
\textbf{sēdecim} (16, "six-ten") and \textbf{septendecim} (17, "seven-ten") keep the same additive pattern.

\begin{culture}
Here's the real oddity. Latin didn't say "eight-ten" or "nine-ten" for 18 and 19 — it counted \textbf{backward from twenty} instead:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{duodēvīgintī} — "\textbf{two FROM twenty}" (18) \textbf{ūndēvīgintī} — "\textbf{one FROM twenty}" (19)
\end{quote}

This is genuinely \textbf{subtractive} counting, not additive — the same logic behind how Latin also names the day before the Kalends. It's a real irregularity sitting right in the middle of an otherwise perfectly additive system. \textbf{Spanish did not inherit this quirk}: \emph{dieciocho} and \emph{diecinueve} are built fresh on the simple "ten-and-X" template, quietly regularizing away something genuinely odd in Latin's own counting.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vīgintī}
\textbf{vīgintī} ("twenty") — the direct, unchanged source of Spanish's \emph{veinte}.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ūndecim, duodecim, tredecim, quattuordecim, quīndecim" — the plain "X-ten" compounds{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "duodēvīgintī, ūndēvīgintī" — 18 and 19, counted BACKWARD from twenty{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vīgintī" — twenty{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item What pattern do \emph{ūndecim} through \emph{quīndecim} follow? (\textbf{Additive} — number + \emph{decim}, "ten.")
  \item What's genuinely odd about Latin's 18 and 19? (They're \textbf{subtractive} — \emph{duodēvīgintī}/\emph{ūndēvīgintī}, literally "two/one FROM twenty," not "eight/nine-ten.")
  \item Did Spanish keep this pattern? (\textbf{No} — \emph{dieciocho}/\emph{diecinueve} use plain addition, regularizing away Latin's quirk.)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
